issues.legal_issue: A magistrate may not require an interim bond or detain a person for refusing it before commencing the inquiry into the truth of the information.
material_facts: The petitioners were arrested without a warrant and brought before a magistrate for preventive proceedings to keep the peace.
The magistrate read them an order requiring them to show cause, then required an interim bond and remanded them when they refused.

Before requiring the bond, the magistrate did not take sworn evidence or otherwise inquire into the truth of the information; the case was adjourned for the petitioners’ statements without witnesses being summoned.
issues.conclusion: The interim-bond proceedings and the resulting detention were illegal because the magistrate had not commenced the inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 117(1)–(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the magistrate must inquire into the truth of the information, and the inquiry is conducted as a trial under the summons-case procedure. The phrase “pending completion of the inquiry” in section 117(3) presupposes that the inquiry has commenced. Before requiring an interim bond, the magistrate must at least begin the inquiry and satisfy himself prima facie about the truth of the information. The Court followed Madhu Limaye v. Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Monghyr.

rule.if: preventive_peace_proceeding and person_brought_before_magistrate and interim_bond_required_before_inquiry_started and person_detained_for_refusing_bond

predicates.preventive_peace_proceeding: The proceeding was brought to require a person to keep the peace or maintain good behaviour.
predicates.person_brought_before_magistrate: The person was brought before a magistrate in that proceeding.
predicates.interim_bond_required_before_inquiry_sta: The magistrate required an interim bond before beginning to inquire into the truth of the information.
predicates.person_detained_for_refusing_bond: The person was detained after refusing to provide the required bond.

issues.definition: When a person is brought before a magistrate in a preventive peace proceeding and is detained for refusing an interim bond required before the inquiry begins, the bond requirement and resulting detention are illegal.

issues.legal_issue: Ordinary powers to secure a person’s later appearance or to adjourn a case do not provide an alternative basis for detaining a person brought before a court under the preventive-proceeding procedure.
material_facts: The petitioners were already in police custody when they were brought before the magistrate under the preventive-proceeding procedure.
The State relied alternatively on ordinary procedural provisions concerning securing attendance and adjournment to support the detention.
The Court held that those provisions did not apply to the petitioners’ situation and that the preventive-proceeding chapter contained its own procedure.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary procedural provisions relied on by the State could not authorize the petitioners’ detention.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply to persons brought before the court under Chapter VIII. Section 91 contemplated a person present in court who was free to appear later, whereas the petitioners were already in custody; section 344 permitted ordinary adjournment arrangements but was not a substitute for section 117(3). The special procedure in Chapter VIII governed.

predicates.preventive_proceeding: The person was brought before the court in a proceeding seeking preventive peace or good-behaviour measures.
predicates.person_already_in_custody_when_brought_b: The person was in custody, rather than free to choose whether to appear, when brought before the court.
predicates.ordinary_appearance_or_adjournment_power: A party relied on an ordinary power for securing later appearance or adjourning a case to justify the detention.

issues.definition: When a person in custody is brought before a court in a preventive proceeding, reliance on an ordinary appearance or adjournment power cannot authorize that person’s detention.

issues.legal_issue: The preventive powers challenged in the petition are constitutionally valid when construed according to the procedural safeguards provided by the governing scheme.
material_facts: The petition challenged the constitutionality of the provision concerning preventive orders and the chapter governing preventive peace proceedings.
A seven-judge Special Bench had already held that those provisions were constitutional and valid when properly construed, and the Court treated the constitutional challenge as concluded.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was concluded by the Special Bench’s holding that the provisions were valid when properly construed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Special Bench’s prior holding that section 144 and Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure are constitutional and valid when properly construed. The judgment does not set out the Special Bench’s full reasoning; it proceeds to apply that construction to the petitioners’ case.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preventive_p: A party challenged the constitutional validity of powers used to prevent anticipated breaches of the peace or public disorder.
predicates.preventive_scheme_construed_with_its_pro: The preventive scheme was construed according to the procedural safeguards governing its use.

issues.definition: When preventive powers are constitutionally challenged and the preventive scheme is construed with its procedural safeguards, the powers are constitutionally valid.
